condition: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset palpitations with breathlessness for the past 5 hours
history: 68-year-old man with a 5-hour history of abrupt-onset irregular palpitations associated with mild exertional breathlessness and light-headedness. No chest pain, syncope, or focal neurological symptoms. Background of hypertension (on amlodipine), type 2 diabetes, and obesity; drinks alcohol at weekends and had a heavier-than-usual intake the previous evening. No prior documented arrhythmia. No fever, cough, or recent illness. Not currently anticoagulated.
examination: Alert and comfortable at rest. Irregularly irregular pulse with a variable-volume apex and a radial pulse deficit. No raised JVP, no basal crackles, no peripheral oedema, heart sounds variable in intensity with no added murmur. No goitre, tremor, or lid lag. Chest clear. Pertinent negatives: no focal neurological deficit, no calf swelling, no signs of decompensated heart failure or shock.
imaging: CXR: clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette, no pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echo (later): mild LA dilatation, preserved LV systolic function, no significant valvular lesion.
differentialDiagnoses: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
finalDiagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (new-onset, likely alcohol/'holiday heart' triggered)
contraindications: Avoid non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers/beta-blocker combination without monitoring
Rate-control caution if occult decompensated HF or pre-excitation (avoid AV-nodal blockers if WPW)
Anticoagulation decision per CHA2DS2-VASc weighed against HAS-BLED bleeding risk
edgeCases: Pre-excited AF (WPW) where AV-nodal blockers can precipitate VF — treat with procainamide/cardioversion
AF as the presenting sign of occult hyperthyroidism, PE, or sepsis — exclude secondary drivers
expectedMaiK: Irregularly irregular tachycardia with a pulse deficit and no P waves points to atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response; prioritise rate control, screen for reversible triggers (alcohol, thyroid, sepsis, PE), and formally assess stroke risk with CHA2DS2-VASc to guide anticoagulation.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact time of symptom onset (guides <48h cardioversion window)?
Any chest pain, syncope, or features of heart failure/haemodynamic compromise?
